title: Is he Santa Claus or Father Christmas? | FESTIVE WORD ORIGINS

entries.note: From Old English Cristes mæsse, Christ's mass or celebration; since the 1500s it has also been used as a verb, to Christmas.
Decorating trees goes back to Roman Saturnalia; people bought them in the 1500s, and German and French law limited people to one tree of no more than eight shoe lengths.

Old English name for the midwinter festival, still with us; its Nordic relatives include [[equivalent:jul]], [[equivalent:jólin]] and Finnish [[equivalent:joulu]], and it is cognate with [[same-root:jolly]].
The name for Christmas in Swedish, Norwegian and Danish, a relative of [[equivalent:Yule]].
Icelandic name for Christmas, in the language closest to Old Norse, related to [[equivalent:Yule]].
Finnish name for Christmas, related to [[equivalent:Yule]]; also found in [[see:joulupukki]].
Yule plus [[from:tide]], an old word related to time.
The tide of [[see:Yuletide]] is an old relative of [[same-root:time]], related to German [[same-root:Zeit]] and Dutch [[same-root:tijd]].
Given as a relative of [[same-root:tide]].
German word cited as related to [[same-root:tide]].
Dutch word cited as related to [[same-root:tide]].
From Old French [[from:jolif]], meaning festive, merry, amorous or pretty, and ultimately from the same Germanic source as [[same-root:Yule]].
The traditional English name for the Christmas gift-giver, preferred by some over the Americanism [[see:Santa Claus]]; compare French [[equivalent:Père Noël]].
An Americanism from the 1700s, a contraction of [[from:St Nicholas]] probably via Dutch [[from?:Sinterklaas]], brought by Dutch-descended New Yorkers; recorded in [[see:Salmagundi]].
The earliest Father Christmas-type figure, from a mid-1400s carol attributed to [[see:Richard Smart]], rector of Plymtree.
Rector of Plymtree, to whom the mid-1400s carol featuring [[see:Sir Christmas]] is attributed.
Original name of the tip of Manhattan, reflecting the Dutch settlement that brought [[see:Santa Claus]] to America.
Periodical [[see:Washington Irving]] and friends started in early-1800s New York to mock society; it records [[see:St Nicholas]] as vulgarly called [[see:Santa Claus]].
Writer who gently mocked Dutch-descended New Yorkers in [[see:Salmagundi]], used Santa Claus, and called [[see:St Nicholas]] the patron saint of New York.
One of [[see:Washington Irving]]'s short stories descended from Dutch folk tales.
[[see:Washington Irving]]'s parody history, in which he called [[see:St Nicholas]] the patron saint of New York.
A mischievous Christmas man of the Tudor and Stuart eras who presided over feasting and entertainment.
Another Tudor and Stuart name for the mischievous Christmas man presiding over feasting, like [[see:Captain Christmas]].
Another Tudor and Stuart personification of Christmas presiding over feasting and entertainment.
[[see:Ben Jonson]]'s 17th-century personification of Christmas, a literal Father Christmas with sons including Misrule, Carol, Mince Pie and Baby Cake.
17th-century playwright who created [[see:Old Gregory Christmas]].
French name for [[equivalent:Father Christmas]], which the English name reflects.
German name for the Christmas gift-giver, literally Christmas man; distinct from [[see:St Nicholas]] in German tradition.
Celebrated on 6 December, traditionally the big gift day in southern Germany; a saint believed Turkish who gave his inheritance to the poor.
Another German Christmas emblem, literally the Christ child, also called [[see:Christkindl]].
Form of [[see:Christkind]] where Kindl means a really little kid; it gave us [[gave:Kris Kringle]].
American name from German [[from:Christkindl]], now an adult figure; popularised by [[see:Miracle on 34th Street]].
Film whose character [[see:Kris Kringle]] is put on trial over claiming to be Santa Claus.
Finnish Father Christmas figure, now a man, named after pre-Christian dressing up as a goat, a fertility symbol; contains [[see:pukki]].
Finnish for goat, related to English [[same-root:buck]] and [[same-root:butcher]].
Related to Finnish [[same-root:pukki]], goat; discussed in other episodes.
Related to Finnish [[same-root:pukki]], goat; discussed in other episodes.
Russian gift-giver resembling Father Christmas who brings presents on New Year's Eve rather than at Christmas.
A greeting much more common in America than Britain, used like [[see:happy holidays]] for inclusion.
In America refers to this time of year; in Britain it means vacation, especially the summer.
Meant as an inclusive greeting, yet literally religious since a holiday is a holy day, echoing German [[see:Weihnachten]].
German name for Christmas, meaning holy nights.
French for Christmas, from Latin [[from:natalis]], birth; sometimes used in English, as in [[see:The First Noel]].
Carol cited as an English use of [[see:Noël]], referring to the birth of Jesus.
Spanish for Christmas, from Latin [[from:natalis]], birth, like [[same-root:Noël]].
Italian for Christmas, from Latin [[from:natalis]], birth, like [[same-root:Noël]].
Japanese for Christmas, taken from the English word.
Japanese name for Santa, adding the polite suffix -san to Santa.

entries.translation: festival of the birth of Christ
entries.note: Russian word for Christmas, meaning a festival of the birth of Christ.
Swahili word for Christmas, from English.
Arabic term for Christmas, the Christian celebration of Jesus's birth, alongside Islam's [[see:Eid al-Fitr]] and [[see:Eid al-Adha]].
One of the two famous eids of Islam, compared with [[see:Eid al-Milad]].
One of the two famous eids of Islam, compared with [[see:Eid al-Milad]].
Modern Greek for Christmas, Christ plus a root meaning birth or generation, the source of [[same-root:gender]], [[same-root:genre]] and [[same-root:generation]].
From the same birth root as the ending of [[same-root:Christougenna]].
From the same birth root as the ending of [[same-root:Christougenna]].
From the same birth root as the ending of [[same-root:Christougenna]].
From Old Norse [[from:hreinn]], reindeer, plus a word for animal; spelled rain deer and range deer before settling, unrelated to harness reins; same species as [[see:caribou]].
Poem known as 'Twas the Night Before Christmas, naming the reindeer; its authorship is disputed between [[see:Clement Clarke Moore]] and [[see:Henry Livingston Jr]].
One of Santa's reindeer named in [[see:A Visit from St Nicholas]]; a self-explanatory name.
One of Santa's reindeer named in [[see:A Visit from St Nicholas]]; a self-explanatory name.
One of Santa's reindeer named in [[see:A Visit from St Nicholas]]; a self-explanatory name.
German for lightning; changed by [[see:Clement Clarke Moore]] from the original Dutch [[from:Blixem]].
One of Santa's reindeer named in [[see:A Visit from St Nicholas]]; a self-explanatory name.
One of Santa's reindeer named in [[see:A Visit from St Nicholas]]; a self-explanatory name.
One of Santa's reindeer named in [[see:A Visit from St Nicholas]]; a self-explanatory name.
German for thunder; originally the Dutch [[from:Dunder]] in the poem, changed by [[see:Clement Clarke Moore]] via an intermediate form.
The reindeer's original Dutch name, paired with [[see:Blixem]], later changed to [[gave:Donner]]; its Dutchness supports [[see:Henry Livingston Jr]]'s claim.
The reindeer's original Dutch name, later changed to German [[gave:Blitzen]].
Claimed authorship of [[see:A Visit from St Nicholas]] and, being of German descent, changed the Dutch reindeer names to [[see:Donner]] and [[see:Blitzen]].
Man of Dutch descent whose family claimed he wrote [[see:A Visit from St Nicholas]], citing the original Dutch reindeer names.
Same species as [[see:reindeer]]; a Canadian French and Mi'kmaq word meaning pawer or scratcher, from digging in snow for food.
Old English mischief-making creature, linked with Christmas from [[see:A Visit from St Nicholas]]; its Germanic root may mean white, relating it to [[same-root?:albino]] and [[same-root?:Alp]].
Little Women author who briefly mentioned Christmas elves in [[see:A Christmas Dream, and How It Came True]].

entries.term: A Christmas Dream, and How It Came True
entries.note: [[see:Louisa May Alcott]]'s children's story, an early mention of Christmas [[see:elf|elves]].
Uncredited 1857 Harper's Weekly poem detailing Santa's workshop full of toy-making elves.
Highly influential women's magazine whose 1873 cover illustration showed modern Christmas elves.
Old English word for a nightmare or sickness, blamed on an [[see:elf]].
Old English term for heartburn, attributed to an [[see:elf]].
German word for a nightmare, essentially an elf dream, discussed in an earlier episode.
Possibly related to [[same-root?:elf]] through a root meaning white.
Possibly related to [[same-root?:elf]] through a root meaning white.
The name means white bumblebee, making it possibly related to [[same-root?:elf]].
Another name for Britain, from the Latin for white, probably after the White Cliffs of Dover; possibly linked to [[same-root?:elf]].
Literally having nothing; went from neutral to negative through [[see:pejoration]], like [[see:villain]].
Once closer to [[see:naive]]: foolish in the 1200s, then fussy, dainty, precise, agreeable, and finally kind and thoughtful by the 1800s.
Compared with the original meaning of [[see:nice]].
A biscuit the hosts guess must be named after the French city of Nice, though neither knows for sure.
Process, discussed before, in which a word's meaning becomes more intense and less pleasant, as with [[see:naughty]] and [[see:villain]].
Once just a peasant or poor farmer, it came to mean the bad guy through use as an insult, like [[see:white trash]].
Compared with [[see:villain]] as a class-based insult.
Originally mistiltan, a [[from:mistle]] twig, with Old English [[from:tān]], twig; nothing to do with toes; linked to [[see:mistle thrush]]es, perhaps through their droppings.
Old name for mistletoe-like plants, sometimes basil; murky Germanic origin, probably referring to a sticky substance, with the OED suggesting a root meaning urine.
Bird fond of mistletoe fruit that spreads it through its droppings; unclear whether it was named after [[see:mistletoe]] or vice versa.
Originally any joyful song sung while ring dancing, from Old French carole, circle dancing; probably from Greek [[from?:chorus]] or [[from?:choraules]], and possibly linked to [[same-root?:corona]].
Greek word given as a possible source of [[gave?:carol]].
A flute player accompanying the choral dance in theatre, a possible source of [[gave?:carol]].
Possibly associated with [[same-root?:carol]] through the idea of rings and roundness, as is [[see:crown]].
Related to [[same-root:corona]], and possibly to [[same-root?:carol]] through roundness.
A round headdress, possibly linked to [[same-root?:carol]] through roundness.
Literally [[from:frank]] incense, meaning true or really good incense; related to the [[see:Franks]].
Now means honest but has an older sense of true, seen in [[gave:frankincense]].
Said to be related to the frank of [[see:frankincense]].
A gum resin like frankincense, Latin murra; its apparently vowelless spelling reflects a Germanic pronunciation of the letter Y.
Another word showing Y must be a vowel, like [[see:myrrh]].
The fart bird, named for the sound its wings make on takeoff, discussed in a previous episode; the main character in [[see:The Twelve Days of Christmas]].
Song about the period from Christmas Day to Epiphany, recorded in [[see:Mirth Without Mischief]], melody from [[see:Frederick Austin]]; the hidden Christian catechism theory is a myth.
The original lyric, misheard as calling birds: blackbirds, collie meaning [[same-root:coal]]-coloured.
The source of the colour sense in [[see:colly birds]].
Nothing to do with reptiles; named turtur after the sound they make.
Possibly from Latin [[see:Gallus gallus]] resembling [[see:Gallic]], or because French hens were prized as big and delicious at Christmas.
Latin name for the chicken, similar to [[see:Gallic]], one explanation for [[see:French hens]].
Term for French people, similar to [[see:Gallus gallus]], offered to explain [[see:French hens]].
1780 book containing the earliest English text of [[see:The Twelve Days of Christmas]].
A French song similar to [[see:The Twelve Days of Christmas]], suggesting the song is older.
English composer who gave [[see:The Twelve Days of Christmas]] its modern melody and lyrics, including the drawn-out five gold rings.
From a Proto-Germanic root meaning short-lasting, implying something pleasant making time fly; it gave the noun [[gave:mirth]].
Noun formed from [[from:merry]] with the [[see:-th]] suffix, as truth from true and strength from strong.
Suffix, discussed before, making nouns from adjectives: [[see:mirth]], [[see:truth]], [[see:strength]], [[see:length]], [[see:breadth]].
Noun from true via [[see:-th]], paralleling [[see:mirth]].
Noun from strong via [[see:-th]], paralleling [[see:mirth]].
Noun from long via [[see:-th]].
Noun from broad via [[see:-th]].
